reviews.text: My first playthrough, I used my decades of experience playing strategy games and some careful thought to buy troops that would compliment each other, place them strategically to support each other, and provide bonuses. My second playthrough, I ignored all of that and bought nothing but zombies. Guess which fared better.

Awesome concept and a fun game but their choices for "balancing" raise some eyebrows. I'm not sure what strategies they're playing with, but there seems to be the idea that you'll be building up a small fortune as you go, even tho not going broke upgrading your troops will catch up to you very fast. I hope the full version is more fun with more troops, but zombie rushing seems to be the way to go. Also, one of the special upgrades is gaining interest on your gold, 1 gold per 10 you have at the start of the turn. If this was just a thing or a commander ability, pretty cool. Yet, it has the drawback of costing you 2 gold every turn. So...it's 1 gold for 30 and then 1 for every 10 after that, otherwise it just hurts you for spending gold. TL;DR it's a fun game, i only struggle with the first commander and it feels like it's just a taste of a pretty fun game

The Good: + Main Gameplay loop is very solid, somewhat unique, and quite fun. The Bad: - "Artstyle" is abysmal. Mobile game MSPaint gradient levels of bad. - Related to that, unit fantasy is terrible. If you know how it feels when an east asian mobile game with flipped assets tries naming units without taking into consideration what assests they have available, it is pretty much this exact feeling. - Active choices in the game are terrible. It does the tradional 'Slay the Spire' "Choose your path" thing, yet there is never really a choice. Same with cards, "relics" and consumables. That whole part of the game needs serious redesign. - Next to no unit variety. (Hopefully just the prologue thing). Going undead? Zombies, ""shamans"" and maybe necromancers. Knights? Lancers. Mages? Shield units and sorcerrers. "Greed"? Scrappers and Mercs. Not only do the clans have no unit variety, you barely have any reason to mix and match, interclan interraction is hillariously broken compared to just looking for a synergy between different clan units.

气在头上，等我先把缺点说完。 一、难度不适合。
你说普通难度是为新手玩家打造，结果我打了8把没一把打过第二个boss。我打尖塔都已经进阶3碎心了，绝对不是我自己有问题。雇佣兵流派看着快400的数值boss几下秒了，英灵流的数值也不够用，那条高吃拐率的破龙开局暴毙，前后排分离（小法师，电法师，盾）也仅仅是打掉第二个boss半血（这还是新手最先解锁的流派）。 二、战场情况不明。
所有单位只有一个模糊的数值，玩家不知道这个数值具体作用到这个单位是多少血多少伤害，导致玩家无法优化自己的属性比例。不是碾压或被碾压的，要么赢得莫名其妙，要么输得莫名其妙。以及敌人的机制不能查看，这对首次游玩体验是致命打击，因为你无法根据敌人调整自己的策略。 三、特殊事件奖励不合理。
你敢信打精英是综合期望最高的吗（哪怕你一定打不过，但是有50以上的血）？算数期望则是赌博第一精英第二。买法术打折我还能理解，但是实际上那点小钱能买的也就一点，还只刷新一次（因为刷新会涨价，再刷新就不划算了）。酒馆更是没20块可自由支配的金币就没必要去，守军更是不如普通商店的兵（连折扣都没有）。 四：内存与体量不够匹配。
上面三点是客观事实，这点是我主观感想。这个游戏的体量不大，还没尖塔的体量大（尖塔起码四个职业都有一套牌），然后吃我2.5g储存。这个游戏到第二章都没有空军，然后基于unity开发，cpu占用也不小（这个不太确定，我只知道我笔记本风扇再响，玩尖塔就不会这样）。开发者真不如换rusted warfare引擎开发（虽然这玩意优化也差，但是非3d的底子优化绝对不会比现在差），又简单又强大，反正别的强大工具像c你们嫌太难了。学学土豆兄弟，打击感强，优化好，demo的可玩性照样比这个游戏强，你们开发个死亡动画就行。 我刚跳出bloon card storm这个垃圾游戏，然后又碰到这个游戏。这倒是提醒我了，忘记给那个游戏差评了，发完这个就给。 改进建议：优化运行与占用，加入更简单的难度，可以查看敌人效果，可以预览单位效果演示（不然就把介绍写详细），优化锁敌（现在前排动不动就让敌人遛到后排） 说几个优点吧：动画做得好，没有白板单位（除了敌人），氛围渲染好，敌人有机制，以及免费要什么自行车，demo不玩白不玩（正式版就算了）。 I'm really frustrated, so let me finish pointing out the flaws first. 1. The difficulty is not suitable. You say the normal difficulty is designed for new players, but I played 8 matches and didn’t get past the second boss once. I’m already at level 3 Shattered Heart in Spire, so it’s definitely not my fault. The mercenary build can usually kill a boss with around 400 stats in a few hits, but the hero builds aren’t strong enough. That high-turn-rate broken dragon dies immediately at the start, and splitting the front and back rows (small mage, electric mage, shield) only manages to take the second boss down to half health (and this is with the first unlocked beginner build). 2. Battlefield information is unclear. All units only have one vague stat; players don’t know exactly how that stat affects the unit’s health or damage, making it impossible to optimize our attribute ratios. It’s neither crushing victory nor crushing defeat—wins and losses feel random. Also, enemy mechanics can’t be viewed, which is a huge blow for first-time players because you can’t adjust strategies based on the enemies. 3. Special event rewards are unreasonable. Can you believe elites supposedly offer the highest expected value (even if you likely can’t win, they still have over 50 health)? By actual expected value, gambling comes first, elite second. I can understand discounted spell purchases, but the amount you can buy isn't much, and it only refreshes once (because the price goes up, and further refreshes aren’t worth it). The tavern isn’t worth visiting unless you have 20 coins to spare, and the garrison units are worse than normal shop troops (they don’t even have discounts). 4. Memory usage doesn’t match the content. The above three points are objective facts; this is my personal opinion. The game isn’t very large, smaller than Spire (Spire at least has four classes with full decks), yet it takes up 2.5GB of storage. By the second chapter, there’s no air unit, and being developed in Unity, the CPU usage is high (I’m not entirely sure, just that my laptop fan went crazy; Spire doesn’t do this). The developers might as well have used the Rusted Warfare engine (though its optimization is also poor, a 2D foundation game is definitely not worse), simple yet powerful, anyway you guys seem to think other strong tools like C are too hard. Take a page from the Potato Bros—strong impact feedback, good optimization, the demo is more playable than this game, you’d only need to add a death animation. I just got out of that lousy game Bloon Card Storm and ran into this one. It reminded me that I forgot to give that game a bad review—will do that after posting this. Suggestions for improvement: optimize performance and resource usage, add an easier difficulty, allow players to view enemy effects, provide unit effect previews (or at least write detailed descriptions), improve targeting (right now front-row units often let enemies slip to the back row). A few pros: the animations are well done, no blank units (except enemies), good atmosphere, enemies have mechanics, and it’s free, so why complain, play the demo if you want (formal version is another matter). ------by microsoft translator

Knightica: Prologue by Mad Mango Games is a compact but thoughtfully constructed introduction to a roguelike auto-battler that leans heavily on planning, synergy, and spatial awareness rather than direct player control. Even in this early slice, the game establishes a clear identity built around preparation and experimentation, inviting players to assemble small tactical squads and then watch their decisions play out in automated combat. It is the kind of design that initially feels straightforward but gradually reveals more nuance as you begin to understand how different systems interact. The core loop revolves around alternating phases of decision-making and execution. Before each encounter, you are given access to a shop where you can recruit units, purchase upgrades, and refine your overall strategy using limited resources. Once your lineup is assembled, you position your units on a grid-based battlefield, carefully considering placement, spacing, and directional orientation. When combat begins, your role becomes entirely observational, as the units act according to their abilities and the outcome is determined by how well you prepared. This structure shifts the focus away from reflexes and toward foresight, rewarding players who can anticipate enemy behavior and build cohesive compositions. What makes the system engaging is the interplay between units and their abilities. Each character brings a distinct function to the battlefield, whether it is absorbing damage, dealing area attacks, or providing support effects. The real depth emerges when these roles begin to overlap and reinforce one another, creating combinations that feel stronger than the sum of their parts. Discovering these synergies becomes the central appeal of the game, encouraging experimentation across multiple runs. The addition of modifiers and enhancements further expands this design space, allowing players to tailor their builds in ways that can drastically alter performance. There is a satisfying sense of discovery in finding a combination that works particularly well, especially when it carries you through increasingly difficult encounters. Despite this strength, the prologue format inevitably limits how far these systems can develop. While individual runs offer a clear sense of progression—starting with basic units and gradually assembling a more refined team—the overall pool of content is relatively small. After several playthroughs, patterns begin to emerge, and the variety of strategies feels more constrained than it initially appears. This does not diminish the quality of the core mechanics, but it does highlight that this is only a preview of a larger intended experience rather than a fully realized game. Another aspect that stands out is the game’s minimal approach to storytelling. The setting suggests a fantasy world filled with conflict and conquest, but these elements remain largely in the background. There is little narrative development or character depth, with the focus instead placed squarely on mechanics and replayability. For players who are primarily interested in strategic systems, this may not be an issue, but those looking for a stronger narrative hook may find the experience somewhat abstract. The lack of story progression means that motivation to continue playing is driven almost entirely by the desire to experiment and improve. Visually, Knightica: Prologue adopts a clean and colorful style that prioritizes clarity. Units are easily distinguishable, and the battlefield is presented in a way that makes positioning decisions intuitive. Animations are simple but effective, ensuring that combat remains readable even when multiple effects are occurring simultaneously. The interface is straightforward and responsive, supporting the game’s strategic focus without unnecessary complexity. While it may not be visually striking in a cinematic sense, it succeeds in delivering a polished and functional presentation that aligns well with its design goals. Replayability is one of the more compelling aspects of the experience. The roguelike structure ensures that each run presents a slightly different set of choices, encouraging players to adapt and experiment with new combinations. Unlockable elements and gradual progression provide additional incentives to continue playing, even within the limited scope of the prologue. However, the longevity of this replayability is tied closely to the available content, and it becomes clear that the full version will need to expand significantly on these systems to maintain long-term engagement. In its current form, Knightica: Prologue stands as a strong proof of concept for a strategic auto-battler that values thoughtful planning and creative problem-solving. Its mechanics are solid, its systems are well-integrated, and its core loop is engaging in short to medium sessions. At the same time, its limited content and lack of narrative depth prevent it from feeling complete, leaving the impression of a game that has more to offer but has not yet fully arrived. For players who enjoy experimenting with builds and optimizing strategies, it provides a satisfying and polished introduction to what could become a much deeper experience. Rating: 7/10
